pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10. Interpret negative numbers in real contexts (temperature, sea level, bank balance) and count forwards and backwards through zero with positive and negative whole numbers; place negatives on a number line and begin to find simple intervals (−4°C rises 7° → 3°C). Extends 'count back through zero' into using and reasoning with negatives.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): 'interpret negative numbers in context, count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): integers and their contexts are formalised in Grade 6 (6.NS.5-7); this is the pre-formal contextual foundation.
• Operational details — Ground negatives in multiple contexts (thermometer, sea level, money) and use the number line to count and to find intervals by 'counting the gap' through zero rather than by rules. Reinforce ordering (−4 < −1) and the meaning of the gap between a negative and a positive (the interval spans zero). Keep it count/interval based; defer formal signed arithmetic.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): places negatives on a line and reads a sub-zero temperature. Tier B (age 9-10, secure): counts through zero and finds a simple rise/fall interval across zero. Tier C (age 10, extending): reasons about intervals spanning zero in context and orders mixed positive/negative sets confidently.
bestPractices: Use several contexts (temperature, sea level, money) so 'negative' is meaningful, not abstract.
Find intervals by counting the gap along the number line THROUGH zero, not by memorised sign rules.
Reinforce ordering across zero (−4 < −1 < 0 < 2) with the line.
Make the zero crossing explicit: the interval from −4 to 3 is 4 up to zero, then 3 more.
Keep to counting/intervals in context; defer formal negative arithmetic to later years.
keyRepresentations: Horizontal number line spanning negatives and positives
Number line 'gap counting' for intervals across zero
Real contexts: temperature change, floors/lifts, bank balance
Ordering strip mixing negatives and positives
commonMisconceptions: Counting the interval across zero wrongly (forgetting the zero step or double-counting it).
Treating a negative as just its digit (ignoring sign).
Applying whole-number intuitions (bigger digit = bigger) to negatives.

learn.summary: For ages 9-10: interpret negative whole numbers in real contexts (temperature, sea level, bank balance), place them on a number line, order mixed positive/negative sets, count forwards and backwards through zero, and find simple intervals that cross zero by counting the gap through zero (e.g. −4°C rising 7° reaches 3°C). Keep the work count- and interval-based in context; defer formal signed arithmetic to later years. Core misconceptions to confront: ordering negatives by magnitude (believing −4 > −1) and miscounting when crossing zero.

activities.title: Count the gap through zero on a thermometer/number line
feedback: If the learner lands on 11, pause: starting at −4 is to the LEFT of (below) zero, so counting 7 steps right/up only reaches 3. Contrast with starting at +4, where 7 steps reach 11.

If the learner lands on 2, check whether they counted the starting value −4 as a jump or counted zero twice; if they land on 4, check whether they skipped zero (jumping straight from −1 to 1). Count the jumps aloud together: −4→−3→−2→−1→0 is exactly four jumps, then 0→1→2→3 is three more; reaching zero takes one jump of its own, so zero is counted once, never skipped and never repeated.
When counting backwards from 3, check that after 0 comes −1, then −2 — the count continues below zero rather than stopping at 0.
When the learner splits the count as '4 up to zero, then 3 more = 7 steps total, landing on 3', confirm they have read the interval positionally rather than by a rule.
For −4°C rising 7°, the interval is 7 degrees (4 up to zero, then 3 more) and the landing value is 3°C.
activities.rationale: Grounding negatives in multiple real contexts and finding cross-zero intervals by counting the gap on the number line (before formal signed arithmetic) makes the zero crossing concrete and directly targets the magnitude-ordering and double-counting errors; counting both forwards and backwards through zero matches the stated standard.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'interpret negative numbers in context, count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero'.
Intervals across zero should be found by counting the gap on the number line through zero, in multiple contexts, before formal signed arithmetic.
learnerActions: Set a starting value in a real context, e.g. the temperature is −4°C, marked on a vertical thermometer or horizontal number line.
Apply a change, e.g. 'it rises by 7 degrees', and move a marker one step at a time, saying each value aloud: −4 → −3 → −2 → −1 → 0, then 1 → 2 → 3.
Deliberately split the count into two parts: how many steps up to reach zero (4), then how many steps beyond zero (3), and record the landing value (3°C).
Count backwards through zero as well: start at 3 and step down in ones — 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2 — saying what comes after 0, so you can move both forwards and backwards across zero.

Switch the SAME line into a different context — sea-level depth or a bank balance — keep the start and change equivalent, and notice the number behaves identically even though it means something different.
State in words where you crossed zero and why the total rise is 7 even though you land on 3.
activities.intendedInsight: An interval that spans zero is found by counting the gap along the line through zero — so many steps up to zero, then so many more beyond — not by a sign rule; you can count both forwards and backwards across zero, and negatives in different contexts behave the same positionally.

activities.title: Order and place mixed negatives and positives
feedback: If the learner places −4 as larger than (to the right of) −1, show both on the line: −4 sits further left/lower, so it is the smaller (colder) value; −7°C is colder than −3°C for the same reason.
Tie the feedback to the context: colder, lower, or more in debt all correspond to being further left on the line and therefore a smaller number.
activities.rationale: Reinforcing ordering across zero with a concrete left-is-less experience confronts the seductive −4 > −1 magnitude error that the research flags as a common misconception.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'interpret negative numbers in context, count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero'.
learnerActions: Arrange a mixed set such as −4, −1, 0, 2, 5 from smallest to largest on a number line.
Place a single value such as −3 at its correct spot on a labelled line.
Decide which of two values is colder/lower/more in debt, e.g. 'Which is colder, −7°C or −3°C?', and justify using position on the line.
Explain why −4 is smaller than −1 even though 4 is a bigger digit than 1, referencing left-is-less on the line.
activities.intendedInsight: On the number line, further left (colder / lower / deeper in debt) means smaller, so −4 < −1 < 0 < 2 < 5 — the size of the digit does not decide the order for negatives.

activities.title: Explain the context (optional spoken/role-play extension)
feedback: Prompt the learner to justify answers by referring to the number line or scale, not just a figure, especially when a change crosses zero.
If a change does not actually cross zero (e.g. −30 m rising to −18 m), confirm that too — not every rise or fall passes through zero.
Keep answers interval/count based; avoid introducing formal signed-arithmetic rules at this stage.
activities.rationale: A character or role-play can motivate multiple real contexts and generate interval questions; the interval reasoning itself is still best grounded on the number line, so this is offered as a contextual extension rather than the primary mechanism.
learnerActions: Take on a role such as a submarine pilot describing depths below sea level, or a weather presenter describing temperature changes.

Pose and answer questions like 'We were at −30 m and rose 12 m — where are we now?' (−18 m, still below the surface) and 'It was −3°C and rose 8° — how warm now?' (+5°C, passing up through zero), and explain the crossing of zero where it happens.
Reason aloud about which depth/temperature is higher or lower and how you know.
activities.intendedInsight: Negatives describe real quantities (depth, temperature, balance); talking through changes rehearses counting through zero in meaningful situations, while noting that not every change actually crosses zero.

constraints: Use several contexts (temperature, sea level, money) so 'negative' is meaningful rather than abstract.
Find intervals by counting the gap through zero on the line, not by memorised sign rules; make the zero crossing explicit (e.g. −4 to 3 is 4 up to zero, then 3 more).
Support counting both forwards and backwards through zero, including stepping down below zero into the negatives.
Keep to counting and intervals in context; defer formal signed arithmetic to later years (US formalises integers in Grade 6; this is the pre-formal contextual foundation).

Ordering and placing tasks (ordering a set, placing on a line, fill-in-the-blank, multiple choice) can assess placement, ordering and simple cross-zero intervals, including the magnitude trap, but selection/recognition responses do not by themselves show the learner can count through zero and construct the reasoning aloud — pair them with the learner explaining their method.

A static thermometer or context poster is a useful reference and can introduce negative readings, but it cannot let the learner step through a changing value; use it as a scaffold alongside an activity where the learner actually counts the gap.
The 1D number line/scale is the natural representation for this topic; a 3D model is not needed here (this is a representation preference for this content, not a general claim that 3D adds nothing).
The role-play/spoken extension is optional and supplementary; do not treat it as a replacement for working on the number line.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source assessment lists distractor 'It is 2°C' while revealedBy says 'Answer is 2 or 4 (an off-by-one at the zero crossing)'. Both off-by-one outcomes (2 and 4) are plausible miscounts; feedback here addresses landing on 2 or 4 rather than asserting a single wrong value.

The original source labelled the 3D representation 'poor' with 'negatives live on a 1D line/scale; 3D adds nothing'. The comparative/necessity 'adds nothing' assertion is not established by the cited sources, so it has been reframed as a representation preference for this topic rather than a universal law.

Arithmetic checked: −4°C rising 7° = 3°C (four steps to zero, three beyond). Sign-stripping error gives 11 (4+7). Off-by-one at zero gives 2 or 4. Counting backwards from 3 through zero gives 3,2,1,0,−1,−2. Role-play examples: −30 m +12 m = −18 m (no crossing); −3°C +8° = +5°C (crosses zero). These are internally consistent and retained for diagnostic feedback.
The CCSS Grade 6 claim and the NCETM guidance claim were marked verified:false in the source; treat their status as unverified in any downstream use.

probeDeeper: Show −4 rising by 7 on a number line — where do you cross zero?
Which is colder, −7°C or −3°C? How does the line show it?
Count backwards from 3 in ones — what comes after 0?
assess.correctAnswer: 3°C. Count up 7 from −4: four steps reach 0, then three more reach 3 — you pass through zero.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the sign and treats −4 as 4: −4 + 7 = 11
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put −4 on a number line to the LEFT of zero; count 7 steps right and see you only reach 3. Contrast with starting at +4.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts across zero — stops at 0, or counts 0 twice
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the jumps aloud on the line: −4→−3→−2→−1→0 is four jumps, not five; zero is a point you pass, not a step you repeat.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer is 2 or 4 (an off-by-one at the zero crossing).

responseLevels.gap: Strips the sign (−4 + 7 = 11) or cannot count through zero.
responseLevels.full: Interprets negatives in context and counts through zero accurately (−4 + 7 = 3), reasoning from number-line position.
responseLevels.partial: Places negatives correctly and orders them, but miscounts by one when crossing zero.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask: 'The temperature is −4°C and it rises by 7 degrees. What is it now, and how did you work it out?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who reads negatives positionally counts up through zero and lands on 3; a child who strips the sign computes 4 + 7 = 11, and one who mishandles zero stalls at 0 or double-counts it. The reason tier reveals how they treat the crossing of zero.
